name: Bhimashankar Temple, Bhimashankar
deity: Shiva as Bhimashankar — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas
period: An ancient Jyotirlinga on the crest of the Sahyadri; the stone temple renewed in the 18th century
dynasty: Older Deccan shrine; Maratha renewal under Nana Phadnavis
summary: High on the forested crest of the Sahyadri, where the Bhima river begins, Bhimashankar honours Shiva as the slayer of the demon Bhima — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, set in a dark stone temple amid mist and woodland.

sections.history: Bhimashankar stands on a ridge of the Sahyadri in the Khed taluka of Pune district, at the head of the valley where the Bhima river rises before flowing east across the Deccan to join the Krishna. The Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram names Bhimashankara among the twelve Jyotirlingas, and the shrine and its river are remembered in literature from about the thirteenth century. The temple of dark stone seen today owes much to the eighteenth century, when the Peshwa minister Nana Phadnavis renewed its assembly hall and spire. A tradition in Assam also honours a Bhimashankar of its own, but it is this mountain shrine that most pilgrims seek. Around it stretches the Bhimashankar Wildlife Sanctuary, home of the Indian giant squirrel.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact, finely built shrine in the Nagara manner, its walls of dark basalt carved with figures and bands of ornament in the tradition of the Deccan builders. A sabhamandap, the hall renewed under Nana Phadnavis, leads to the sanctum, where the Jyotirlinga rests. Above it rises the curved spire of the eighteenth-century renewal. Close to the temple hangs a great bell associated with the Maratha general Chimaji Appa, brought here after the Vasai campaign of 1739.
sections.legends: The sacred story tells of Bhima, a mighty demon said to be the son of Kumbhakarna, who grew arrogant through boons and turned on the gods and the devout. When he attacked a king absorbed in the worship of Shiva, the lord appeared from the linga itself and destroyed him. Answering the prayers of the gods and sages, Shiva remained on this mountain as Bhimashankar. Tradition adds that the sweat of the lord after the battle flowed down the hill and became the Bhima river.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great day, when pilgrims climb through the night and a fair gathers around the temple. The Mondays of Shravan, falling in the monsoon, draw devotees through mist and rain, and Kartik Purnima, honoured as Tripuri Purnima, is also kept with lamps and worship. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Bhimashankar rewards those who arrive slowly. The road climbs through the forest of the Ghats, and in the rains the temple is wrapped in cloud. A flight of steps leads down to the shrine, set in a hollow below the village. Many pilgrims also walk to Gupt Bhimashankar, where the Bhima is said to begin, and listen for the call of the giant squirrel in the sanctuary woods.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night, with aartis through the day; crowds are heaviest at Maha Shivaratri, on Shravan Mondays and on monsoon weekends. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctum; follow the posted rules and staff guidance in and around the temple.
visit.gettingThere: Bhimashankar is about 110 km from Pune by road, by way of Rajgurunagar (Khed) and Manchar, through the hills of the Western Ghats; Pune is the nearest railway station and airport. Experienced walkers also climb up the Ghats from the Karjat side.
